summary: Explains the IPv6 subnet model, particularly that an IPv6 address is not automatically tied to an on-link prefix. Incorrect implementations caused interoperability and security problems. It updates part of the definition of on-link from RFC 4861. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Having a house number does not mean the whole street is next door. This clears up a common mistake about which addresses are directly reachable.

questions: what does on-link mean in ipv6
does an ipv6 address imply an on-link prefix
what did rfc 5942 change in rfc 4861
subtitle: In IPv6, having an address does not mean its subnet is on your link; this RFC spells out the rules.

tldr.problem: IPv4 habits tie an address to a netmask and so to an on-link prefix, but IPv6 does not. Hosts that assumed otherwise failed to interoperate and, in some cases, had security problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that on-link status comes only from explicit information such as Router Advertisements with the L-bit set, manual configuration or Redirects. It deprecates two bullets of the 'on-link' definition in RFC 4861.
tldr.outcome: Hosts must not invent an on-link prefix from an assigned address. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4861.

facts.label: Deprecated on-link tests
facts.value: 2 bullets (NA received, any ND message received)

facts.label: Invented prefix seen in the wild

today: RFC 5942 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4861, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its deprecation of the last two on-link bullets is part of the on-link definition it modifies.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Subnet Models
sections.content:
In IPv4, assigning an address to an interface normally also means giving a netmask. The address and netmask together define an on-link prefix, and traffic to addresses in it goes directly rather than to a router. Before subnetting (RFC 950) and CIDR (RFC 4632), the netmask could be derived from the address class, and some implementations still fall back to that.

IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) works differently. The on-link determination is separate from address assignment. A host can have addresses with no related on-link prefix, or on-link prefixes unrelated to its addresses. By default a host treats only the link-local prefix as on-link.

Getting this wrong can cost IPv6 connectivity, and the RFC says incorrect handling also raised security concerns.
sections.eli5: In the old system, your address came with a built-in guess about who lives nearby. In the new one, the address says nothing about neighbors.

sections.title: How a Host Learns What Is On-Link
sections.content:
An IPv6 address is on-link for a specific link if it is assigned to an interface attached to that link. But a host only knows a destination is on-link if it has been told. There are two main mechanisms.

  • The Prefix List holds on-link prefixes. It is filled by a valid Router Advertisement with a prefix whose L-bit is set, which is on-link for its Valid Lifetime, or by manual configuration, which may even be a /128. The link-local prefix is effectively a permanent entry.
  • Redirects can mark individual destinations as on-link by updating the Destination Cache. This happens when the Target and Destination Address of the Redirect are the same.

ND has no way to say a destination is off-link. A destination is assumed off-link unless explicit information says otherwise, and that information can expire. Redirects only name a better next hop and do not mark anything off-link.
sections.eli5: You only treat a house as next door if someone gave you a list saying so, or pointed it out. Everyone else is assumed to be far away.

sections.title: The Update to the On-Link Definition
sections.content:
RFC 4861 said a node considers an address on-link if a Neighbor Advertisement was received for it, or if any Neighbor Discovery message was received from it. This RFC deprecates and removes both of those two bullets. Neither should be used to change the Prefix List or Destination Cache.

The reason is that adding an address to the Neighbor Cache is intentional, but is not the same as calling it on-link. A node creates a STALE Neighbor Cache entry on a valid Neighbor Solicitation (NS), to save a round of address resolution. Since that address is not validated, an intruder could spoof one for a remote site. This is harmless while the entry stays only in the Neighbor Cache. It becomes a problem if the forwarding code then treats the address as on-link.

Text in Sections 7.2.3 and 6.2.6 of RFC 4861 that creates Neighbor Cache entries remains consistent. NS, NA or Router Solicitation may update the Neighbor Cache, but the Prefix List must not change.
sections.eli5: Hearing a stranger shout your name does not make them your neighbor. You can write their name in a notebook, but you should not assume they live next door.

sections.title: Rules for Correct Hosts
sections.content:
A correctly implemented IPv6 host MUST follow these rules.

  • Assigning an address, by SLAAC (RFC 4862), DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) or manual configuration, MUST NOT implicitly cause a prefix derived from it to be treated as on-link.
  • If an RA advertised a prefix with the L-bit set and its Valid Lifetime later expires, the host MUST update its Prefix List. Usually the addresses go back to off-link, although another Prefix List entry may still cover them.
  • If the Default Router List is empty and there is no other on-link information, the host MUST NOT assume all destinations are on-link and MUST NOT perform address resolution for non-link-local addresses. It should instead send an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable indication, as in RFC 4943.

On-link information about particular prefixes does not change this default for everything else.
sections.eli5: Do not assume a neighbor just because of your own address. If you have no helper who knows the way, say 'can't get there' instead of shouting around the block.

sections.title: Observed Incorrect Behavior
sections.content:
The RFC describes one failure seen in several popular host operating systems. In an access concentrator network (RFC 4388), a host gets an RA with no on-link prefix. It acquires an address through DHCPv6 IA_NA, which has no prefix length, or through manual configuration without one. The host then assumes an invented prefix, typically a /64 supplied as a default by the operating system's API, is on-link.

This can seem to work with SLAAC, but in Non-Broadcast Multi-Access (NBMA) networks the host tries address resolution when it should send non-link-local traffic to a default router. Nobody answers, so the host cannot send IPv6 traffic.

The RFC also says multihomed hosts must keep ND processing local to each link. An NS for an address assigned only to a different link must not be answered, and an NA goes out the link the NS arrived on.
sections.eli5: Some computers guessed that a whole block of addresses were next door. Nobody there answered, so their messages never got out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document addresses a security concern in RFC 4861, and the two deprecated bullets are the fix. The security problem for NS was found by David Miles and the same problem for Router Solicitation by Jinmei Tatuya. The RFC states that US-CERT Vulnerability Note VU#472363 lists the affected implementations.

The concern fits the broad set of attacks possible by an on-link neighbor, discussed in RFC 3756.
sections.eli5: If anyone could trick you into thinking a faraway address was next door, they could mislead your traffic. Dropping the guessing rules closes that door.
